s6.p1: So, using the **⟦f0⟧** constructor, you can create a magic box with two holes.
s6.p2: As we’ve already seen, it’s simply impossible to look inside this box ‘here and now’.
s6.p3: Access to its contents is only possible via the [►►►**Event Loop**►►►](⟦f10⟧).
s6.p4: In other words, you’ll have to send a callback to retrieve the result; there’s no other way to extract the contents from the box.
s6.p5: Let’s work out exactly why this is the case.
s6.p6: In fact, the **⟦f0⟧** instance acts as a ‘trap’ for the result of the asynchronous process.
s6.p7: As we do not know when the asynchronous process will finish, we do not know when the state of the box will change and its contents will appear.
s6.p8: If the box could be opened straight away, we would most likely see an empty box.
s6.p9: Now imagine that you are hanging around the box, waiting for its contents to appear.
s6.p10: In other words, you are blocking the call stack.
s6.p11: But the contents cannot appear in the box whilst the call stack is busy.
s6.p12: Even if the server’s response has already arrived, or the timer has expired...
s6.p13: In other words, you’ll be left holding an empty box. And you’ll block the page in the process.
s6.p14: Conclusion: the code that created the instance **⟦f0⟧** must terminate and free up the call stack.
s6.p15: When we pass our callbacks to the **⟦f0⟧** instance via the ‘holes’ **⟦f4⟧**, **⟦f5⟧** and **⟦f6⟧**, we free up the call stack and allow the box to obtain the required result. Once it has received the result, the box will pass it to one of our callbacks.
